editorialIntro: Most teams don't have an AI problem. They have twelve half-ideas and no way to rank them. The Strategy Sprint replaces that noise with a scored, sequenced plan: where AI earns its keep, in what order, and what to leave alone.

editorialSections.title: Owners and operators who are done guessing

blocks.text: You run a small or mid-size business, a professional practice, or a team inside a larger org. You keep hearing that you should "use AI," you've tried a few things, and none of it has stuck. You don't need another demo. You need someone to look at how you actually operate and tell you the truth about where this technology pays off and where it will waste your money.

items: You have 5–200 people and real workflows worth mapping.
You want a decision, not a science project.
You'd rather spend two weeks getting it right than two quarters drifting.

editorialSections.title: Adoption stalls when nobody has ranked the work

blocks.text: Without a roadmap, AI spending scatters. One person builds a clever prompt, another buys a tool nobody adopts, a third pilot quietly dies. There's no shared view of which processes are high-volume, low-risk, and genuinely improvable — the only combination worth automating first.

The Sprint fixes the sequencing problem. We inventory your workflows, score each candidate on impact, effort, and risk, and hand you an ordered plan. You stop spreading effort thin and start compounding wins in the right order.

editorialSections.title: A structured audit, run with you

blocks.text: Discovery interviews
Two to four working sessions with you and the people who own the workflows, so the plan reflects how the business really runs — not an org chart.
Workflow inventory
A mapped list of repeatable processes across your team, with volume, time cost, and sensitivity noted for each.
Opportunity scoring
Every candidate scored on impact, effort, and risk using a transparent rubric you keep. No black boxes.
Risk and guardrail review
A first pass on where confidentiality, accuracy, or disclosure obligations mean AI needs limits — or shouldn't be used at all.
Tooling recommendation
A grounded view of which tools fit your budget, data posture, and team, with honest trade-offs.
Roadmap readout
A live walkthrough of the sequenced plan so your team leaves aligned, not just emailed a PDF.

editorialSections.title: What you keep at the end

items: A written AI roadmap: prioritized initiatives, sequenced across the next one to three quarters.
The scored opportunity matrix, so you can re-rank as things change.
A tooling shortlist with fit notes and rough cost ranges.
A one-page risk summary flagging where to slow down or bring in a professional.
A recorded readout and your slides, yours to keep and share internally.

blocks.text: You own everything. If you never work with us again, the roadmap still stands on its own. That's the point.
One-week focused audit
A single workflow area or department. Fastest path to a decision when the scope is already narrow.
Two-week standard Sprint
The default. Full workflow inventory, scoring, risk pass, and readout across the business.
Three-week extended Sprint
Adds deeper stakeholder interviews and a light proof-of-concept on the top-ranked workflow, so you see it work before you commit to a build.

editorialSections.title: Where the Sprint pays off — and where it doesn't

blocks.text: Great fit: a services firm, agency, clinic, or operations team with recurring manual work and a genuine intent to change how it runs. You have a budget owner in the room and can commit a few hours of your team's time over two weeks.

Not the right fit yet: if you already know exactly what to build and just need it built, skip the Sprint and go straight to Workflow Design or Implementation. If you're just curious, the free University will take you a long way first.

editorialIntro: Two people quietly using AI well doesn't move a business. Everyone using it competently — and knowing when to stop — does. These are live, hands-on workshops built around your team's real work, so people leave with skills they'll use on Monday.

blocks.text: Some of your people are already using AI. Most aren't, or are using it timidly and inconsistently. You want a common baseline: everyone confident with the tools you actually use, working from the same rules, producing work you'd be comfortable putting your name on.

items: You have a team of roughly 5 to 50 who'd benefit from shared skills.
You want practice on your work, not slides about someone else's.
You care as much about judgment — when not to use AI — as about mechanics.

blocks.text: The webinar everyone half-watches teaches AI in the abstract, so nobody knows how it applies to their inbox, their reports, their client work. People nod along, close the tab, and change nothing. Worse, untrained enthusiasm creates real risk: confidential data pasted into the wrong tool, hallucinated facts shipped to clients, no one checking anything.
These workshops fix both problems. We train on your workflows with your examples, so the skills stick — and we teach the guardrails alongside the techniques, so confidence doesn't outrun judgment.
